payload.reason: Composed from one proposal (practice). It was selected against Q-078 (a person's decision), the three spikes and the build-check's measured constraints. No other proposal contested it.
payload.selection_rationale:
The practice proposal does what the person decided in Q-078 (human): after each ItemsSource swap, re-select the row by its folder path and refocus its new container in the Loaded-priority callback that restores the scroll. The menu's Tag/CommandTarget=Window workaround stays. Reality measured this exact shape as go: spike 3 held 240/240 refreshes, including under 8-of-16-CPU load, against a baseline of 0/240, and an Input-priority press queued straight after the swap ran once on the right row 30/30 per process.

The brief named another approach: keep containers alive with an in-place keyed diff and Move-based reorder. Reality measured that no-go twice:
- Spike 1: S3 0/10 and S4 3/10, because a Move of the focused item disconnects its container.
- Spike 2: on the real MainWindow the focused container was replaced at r3, and the unchanged repro cannot run at all against wrapper items (precondition throw at :100).

The proposal also fits how the code is already built:
- ShowTopLevel already assigns one new sorted TopLevelRow[] per snapshot.
- TopLevelRow is immutable and reference-equal.
- Four readers walk TopLevelList.Items as TopLevelRow: the SL-100 repro, the SL-063 tests, WindowReport.cs:247 and the hook. None of them changes.
- About 25 lines go into a callback that already exists, so the change is cheap to reverse.

The practice designer raised over_engineering_flag against the popular MVVM answer, against their own interest. Both the spikes and Q-078 back that flag.

The bug report was only a title. I assumed the scope is Q-078, plus derived criteria 2-4, plus the half of SC-181 the loop can check (the acceptance command runs on the net10.0-windows build).

Derived criteria 1 and 5 (containers survive the refresh, and the Tag/CommandTarget pattern becomes unnecessary) came from a model reflection. A person's answer outranks them, so they are recorded as not met by decision Q-078. They are neither built nor treated as missing.

Process note for the reviewer: the slice is tiered low, so the critique is skipped. Lessons #337 and #186 say a slice that touches MainWindow rows and gestures should not be tiered low. Nothing here has yet survived a disagreement.

components.name: Row-key capture before the swap
components.responsibility:
Runs in ShowTopLevel immediately before `TopLevelList.ItemsSource = rows` (MainWindow.xaml.cs:386). Results go into closure locals only, with no new fields.
- selectedKey = (TopLevelList.SelectedItem as TopLevelRow)?.Path.
- Keyboard.FocusedElement is a ListBoxItem whose ItemsControl.ItemsControlFromItemContainer is TopLevelList and whose DataContext is a TopLevelRow: wantFocus=true, focusKey=that row's Path.
- Keyboard.FocusedElement is TopLevelList itself (a previous restore could not realise the row, or the person tabbed onto the list): wantFocus=true, focusKey=selectedKey.
- Anything else (an open row menu, the Cancel button, another list, another window, or null while the window is inactive): wantFocus=false.
components.key_interactions: Reads only public WPF state and TopLevelRow.Path. It does not touch Core, TopLevelTracker or the scan store. The snapshot channel compared by ReferenceEquals (lesson #133) and the rule that the window never touches the scan store are unchanged.

components.name: Restore by key in the existing Loaded callback
components.key_interactions: Loaded (6) runs after layout and before Input (5) and the next timer tick (Background, 4). The extra work falls inside _refreshClock, so the SL-039 SlowRefresh skip (100 ms, :42) still sees what it costs (lesson #134). The repaired Keyboard.FocusedElement.DataContext makes OnCanOpenInExplorer, OnOpenInExplorer and PathOf (:776-852) resolve the row again; those three are unchanged.

components.name: Context-menu workaround (kept unchanged)
components.key_interactions: An open menu holds keyboard focus, so the capture records wantFocus=false and the refresh never moves focus out of a menu. Containers still detach, so R-001 top-live (WindowCases.ps1:4009, RevealMode.cs:282-295) still sees detached==true and sentinel==true.

contracts.name: ShowTopLevel survives the Reset
contracts.notes:
For the `rows` array it assigned, by the time ShowTopLevel's Loaded callback has run:
- If a row with the remembered selected Path exists in `rows`, that row is SelectedItem.
- Suppose keyboard focus was on a TopLevelList row container, or on TopLevelList itself, before the swap, and is on TopLevelList itself at the callback. If the row's container is realised at the restored offset, focus is now on that container.
- The scroll offset is the one restored before the swap. The restore never scrolls.
- ItemsSource is still a new TopLevelRow[] per snapshot. The swap still happens and old containers still detach.
contracts.error_cases:
- Key not present in the new rows: no selection is set and focus is not moved.
- Row outside the restored viewport (ContainerFromItem null after one UpdateLayout): the row stays selected and focus stays on the ListBox. A later refresh that realises the row refocuses it.
- ItemsSource replaced or nulled before the callback (ShowFolderTree, ClearTopLevel, a later ShowTopLevel): no restore at all.
- Focus anywhere else (open menu, button, another control, null): focus is never moved.

contracts.name: Ctrl+Enter on a results row across a live refresh
contracts.notes: The OpenInExplorer KeyGesture, its Window CommandBinding, OnCanOpenInExplorer, OnOpenInExplorer and PathOf are all unchanged. After the Loaded callback, Keyboard.FocusedElement.DataContext is the current TopLevelRow, so CanExecute is true and the command runs exactly once on that row. A key queued at Input priority straight after the swap runs after the restore (spike 3, 30/30 per process).
contracts.error_cases:
These gaps are recorded rather than designed around:
- A focused row pushed out of view has a dead Ctrl+Enter until it is visible again.
- A real keystroke in the swap-to-Loaded gap (SC-254) is not measurable here.
- The first press after returning from Explorer depends on where WPF's reactivation puts focus. That is filed for a person.

contracts.auth_model: person-run: it opens and drives real Explorer windows on the desktop (lesson #336). No loop stage runs it.

key_decisions.decision: Restore by key after the Reset, as Q-078 (human) decided, instead of keeping containers alive with an in-place keyed diff.
key_decisions.rationale: The person decided this, and the measurements agree. Spike 3 was go: 240/240 under load, baseline 0/240. Spikes 1 and 2 were no-go, because ObservableCollection.Move of the focused row disconnects its container (S3 0/10; real app at r3). The only Move variant that held, moving the other rows past the focused one, ran on a stand-in, and it still needs a wrapper item type that breaks four readers. The restore is about 25 lines in an existing callback.

key_decisions.decision: Derived 1 and Derived 5 (containers not detached; row actions no longer need Tag/CommandTarget=Window) are recorded at validate as 'not met by decision Q-078'. They are not treated as missing. The menu workaround stays, R-001's detached==true stays true, and lesson #187 still binds future row actions.
key_decisions.rationale: The brief's 'diff the list / preserve items' came from SL-047's reflection, which is a model. Q-078 is a person's answer that keeps the menu workaround and holds in-place diffing back 'only if a later row action needs containers living across refreshes'. No such action exists in the tree. Reversing this later means rewriting the SL-039 refresh path and migrating the item type that four readers depend on.

key_decisions.decision: Items stay TopLevelRow, and ItemsSource is still a new sorted array per snapshot.
key_decisions.rationale: The unchanged repro, the SL-063 tests, WindowReport.cs:247 and the hook all read Items as TopLevelRow. Spike 2 showed the unchanged repro cannot even reach its assertion on wrapper items.

key_decisions.decision: The row key is TopLevelRow.Path, compared with StringComparison.Ordinal.
key_decisions.rationale: Build-check constraint 3 says Name and Path are the only identity across snapshots. Row i is always root child _first+i, so Path is stable within a scan. Case-sensitive folders can hold siblings that differ only by case (lesson #327), and OrdinalIgnoreCase would pick the wrong one.

Loaded runs after layout and ahead of Input and the next Background tick, so queued keystrokes see the restored focus. Spike 2's r3 run with its Loaded fallback showed the repro's refresh-then-press sequence presses after Loaded work has run; the adapted test changed only item addressing. That is the basis for keeping the unchanged Fact.

UpdateLayout goes after the scroll restore, not as a retry when the container is null (practice's order). Otherwise a container realised at the pre-restore offset could be focused, kept realised out of view by recycling, and pulled back into view by Focus(), which fights the restore. Doing it before LastRefresh keeps the restore's cost inside the droppable-refresh timing (lesson #134).

key_decisions.decision: Focus moves only from TopLevelList itself onto the row, and only when the list or one of its rows had focus before the swap. The refresh never calls ScrollIntoView or BringIntoView, so a row outside the restored viewport stays selected but unfocused.
key_decisions.rationale: The worst regression a refocus can cause is stealing focus every 250 ms: from an open row menu (which would close it and break SL-047's menu and R-001), from the Cancel button, or from another list. Requiring focus to be exactly where WPF drops it rules all of those out. Not scrolling keeps the existing rule that a refresh never moves the person's viewport.

key_decisions.decision: The restore keeps its state in closure locals and does nothing unless TopLevelList.ItemsSource is still the array it was scheduled for. No new fields are added.
key_decisions.rationale: ShowFolderTree, ClearTopLevel and ShowFinalTopLevel can run at Normal priority between a tick's swap and its Loaded callback. A guarded closure can never apply one list's key to another, or to a null ItemsSource, and leaves nothing to clear on a new scan.

key_decisions.decision: No KnownWorkarounds entry and no settings checkbox.
key_decisions.rationale: The defect is this project's own code: ShowTopLevel replaces ItemsSource wholesale every 250 ms. WPF's container unlinking, focus fallback to the ancestor and reference-based selection are documented by-design behaviour, not an outside defect (investigation; BindingOperations.DisconnectedSource docs). A bug in this project's own code is fixed, never toggled.

key_decisions.decision: Q-078's window case ('select row mid-scan, wait 3 refreshes, Ctrl+Enter, expect reveal') is built as a person-run R-001 step backed by a hook step. The loop's evidence is the in-process Facts on the real MainWindow.
key_decisions.rationale: 'Expect reveal' opens real Explorer, which only a person may run (lesson #336). R-001 already keeps a scan live and opens and closes Explorer. A loop-run copy that skipped the reveal would duplicate the xUnit proof.

key_decisions.decision: Logical focus (FocusManager) while the window is inactive is not handled. A refresh that runs while Explorer has the foreground captures nothing.
key_decisions.rationale: Q-078 scopes the refocus to 'if the list had keyboard focus', and an inactive window has none. Where WPF's reactivation puts focus is recalled, not measured. If it lands on the ListBox, the next tick's 'focus is on the list itself' branch refocuses the selected row. If not, the gap is filed as a person check with a follow-up slice, not guessed at here.

proposals.note:
The only proposal. All of its pieces were taken. Two seams were redesigned:
- UpdateLayout now always runs after the scroll restore before ContainerFromItem (practice tried ContainerFromItem first and laid out only on a null result).
- The case matrix grew from three Facts to ten shapes: an open menu, no keyboard focus, a row pushed out of view, a replaced list, a key queued in the gap, an unchanged row, and arrow navigation.
The R-001 step's wording no longer claims it judges SC-181.

payload.coherence_check:
There was one proposal, so there is no composition to check. Nothing in this design has yet survived a disagreement, and the reviewer is the first to argue with it.

Checked against reality instead:

(1) Q-078 against the brief. Q-078 (human) contradicts Derived 1 and 5 from the build-check, which came from a model reflection. The person's answer wins and is not built twice. Q-078 contradicts no measurement: spikes 1 and 2 confirm its reasoning and spike 3 measured its shape go.

(2) Build-check constraints 1-3 hold under the design:
- Containers still detach, so R-001 top-live's detached==true (WindowCases.ps1:4009) stays true.
- Items stay TopLevelRow, so the SL-063 tests, WindowReport.cs:247 and the hook are unaffected.
- The key is Path, the stable identity.

(3) The restore runs at Loaded priority, which is the person's stated priority. Spike 2's r3 run shows the unchanged repro presses after Loaded work.

(4) The capture rule records wantFocus=false whenever an open menu holds focus, so SL-047's menu workaround and the refocus cannot fight. The AnOpenRowMenuSurvivesARefresh Fact settles the recalled claim behind this.

Changed at a seam: practice called ContainerFromItem first and UpdateLayout only on null. That could focus a container realised at the pre-restore offset, which recycling keeps alive out of view and which Focus() would then bring back into view against the restored offset. It is now scroll restore, then reselect, then UpdateLayout (only when a focus restore is wanted), then ContainerFromItem, with null meaning 'out of view, leave focus on the list'.

architecture_rules is deliberately empty:
- The design adds no dependency. The window still never touches the scan store, and Core is untouched.
- Its invariants are behavioural: no focus steal, no scroll, an Ordinal key, a stale-array guard. None of them can be written as a regex without firing on correct code elsewhere in MainWindow.xaml.cs.
- The DisconnectedSource comparison rule belongs to SL-047's settlement, not this design's.
- Every rule the engine appends has a measured cost on this project: harness rows, settled counts, and silent RuleCases reds (lessons #212, #273, #328).

The workaround-setting policy does not apply. The defect is this project's own ItemsSource replacement, and WPF's behaviour is documented by-design.

cases.behaviour: press Ctrl+Enter on the focused results row during a live scan
cases.shape: the focused row is still being read, so the tracker rebuilds it as a new TopLevelRow object at the refresh (the captured failure)
cases.why: Selector keeps a selection only by reference, so a rebuilt row loses it (SelectedIndex -1). Focus drops to the ListBox, whose DataContext is null, so CanExecute is false. The restore has to find the row by Path, not by object.
cases.check: pwsh -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File eng/dotnet.ps1 test tests/bugs/SL-100-ResultsListRefresh/SL-100-ResultsListRefresh.Tests.csproj  (original Fact CtrlEnterOnTheFocusedRowStillWorksAfterTheLiveRefresh, unchanged)

cases.behaviour: press Ctrl+Enter on the focused results row during a live scan
cases.shape: the focused row did not change, so the tracker kept the same object and its selection survives the Reset by itself
cases.why: The reselect step is a no-op here, but the new container still has no focus (probe case A). Code that returns early when SelectedItem already matches would leave Ctrl+Enter dead on every unchanged row.

cases.behaviour: press Ctrl+Enter on the focused results row during a live scan
cases.shape: three refreshes in a row; on the second, the rebuilt focused row grows past the largest row and moves to index 0
cases.why: Spikes 1 and 2 broke exactly at the refresh where the focused row's index changed. The key must not depend on the index, and the restore must hold on every refresh, not only the first. After each refresh Ctrl+Enter must run exactly once on the current row object.

cases.behaviour: move through the results list with the arrow keys after a refresh
cases.shape: Down is pressed on the restored row
cases.why: A programmatically selected item whose container is not focused sends arrow keys from the list, so Down jumps to the first row (SO 7363777). Only a focused container makes Down go to the next row.

cases.behaviour: keep my place in the results list through a refresh
cases.shape: the focused row is below the first screenful and the list is scrolled
cases.why: After the Reset the realised containers belong to the pre-restore offset. The row's container exists only once the restored offset is laid out, so UpdateLayout must come after the scroll restore. VerticalOffset must end where it was before the refresh. Spike 3's 20-row probe never scrolled.

cases.behaviour: keep my place in the results list through a refresh
cases.shape: a reorder pushes the focused row out of the restored viewport, and a later refresh brings it back into view

cases.behaviour: use other controls while a scan runs
cases.shape: keyboard focus is on a focusable control outside the list (the Cancel button) while a row is selected
cases.why: A refocus that fired on any focus would steal it every 250 ms. Focus must stay on the control, and the selected row must still be reselected.

cases.behaviour: use other controls while a scan runs
cases.shape: nothing has keyboard focus (Keyboard.ClearFocus before the refresh, standing in for an inactive window)
cases.why: Keyboard.FocusedElement is null. The capture must not throw or take focus, and selection is still restored.

cases.behaviour: open a row's context menu during a live scan
cases.shape: the row's ContextMenu is open when the refresh runs
ClearTopLevel or ShowFolderTree replaces the list between a tick's swap and its Loaded callback
cases.why: Without the ReferenceEquals(ItemsSource, rows) guard, the restore would select a row of a list that is gone, or hit a null ItemsSource or container. The Fact runs ShowTopLevel, then ClearTopLevel before pumping, then pumps. Expected: no exception, no selection, focus untouched.

cases.behaviour: press Ctrl+Enter on the focused results row during a live scan
cases.shape: the key press is queued at Input priority in the same tick, straight after the swap, before the restore has run
cases.why: This is the closest machine-checkable stand-in for a keystroke arriving in the gap. The restore must run at a priority above Input. Spike 3 measured this on a stand-in only, never on the real MainWindow.

cases.behaviour: read the results list as rows (revised marks, report, hook)
cases.shape: existing readers enumerate TopLevelList.Items as TopLevelRow across live refreshes
cases.why: The item type is a contract with four readers. The refresh path change must not alter it, and SL-063's done-row finality must still hold.

cases.shape: Cancel's ShowFinalTopLevel runs between a tick's swap and its Loaded callback, and the focused row had just been rebuilt
cases.why: The guard rightly skips the tick's restore. The final ShowTopLevel then sees focus already on the ListBox and the selection already lost, so the stopped list shows no selection. Judged not worth a test: the window is a few ms per 250 ms tick and only on Cancel, a click restores the row, and there is no deterministic trigger without a seam. The fix, if wanted, is the filed SelectedItem fallback.

cases.behaviour: keep my place in the results list through a refresh
cases.shape: two root children whose names differ only by case (a case-sensitive folder)
cases.why: Ordinal comparison picks the exact row; OrdinalIgnoreCase would pick the first case sibling (lesson #327). Judged not worth a test: it needs a case-sensitive NTFS directory or synthetic rows the tracker does not produce from a plain temp tree, and the choice is one comparison argument.

outside_claims.claim: Assigning a new ItemsSource to a WPF ListBox is a Reset. Inside the assignment itself, every item container is unlinked: its DataContext becomes BindingOperations.DisconnectedSource and it leaves the visual tree.
outside_claims.source: Investigation probe .taad-scratch/focusprobe, case A1, on Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App 10.0.12 on this PC. Spike 3 baseline, 320/320 refreshes.
outside_claims.if_wrong: Nothing in this design; it is the cause the repro already captured.

outside_claims.claim: When the keyboard-focused ListBoxItem leaves the tree, keyboard focus moves to the ListBox itself, the nearest focusable ancestor, at the assignment. It stays there through layout and idle.
outside_claims.source: Investigation probe A1-A3. Spike 3 sync snapshot: ListBox 640/640. Repro: 'keyboard focus on ListBox (DataContext null)'.
outside_claims.if_wrong: The refocus trigger 'Keyboard.FocusedElement is exactly TopLevelList' would never fire. Every focus Fact goes red and the restore needs a different trigger.

outside_claims.claim: Selector keeps SelectedItem across a Reset only if the same object is in the new items. A rebuilt row leaves SelectedIndex at -1.
outside_claims.source: Investigation probe case B. Repro output 'list SelectedIndex -1'.
outside_claims.if_wrong: Reselect-by-key would be redundant, but harmless.

outside_claims.claim: A Dispatcher callback queued at Loaded priority during the tick runs before work queued at Input priority after the swap.
outside_claims.source: Spike 3: Loaded callback came before the gap press, which came before the idle snapshot, 30/30 per process across 4 processes.
outside_claims.if_wrong: A press queued in the gap would route from the ListBox and be lost. The restore would have to run synchronously inside ShowTopLevel.

outside_claims.claim: A real hardware keystroke arriving between the swap and the Loaded callback is dispatched after that callback. The dispatcher processes items above Input priority before it dispatches queued input.
outside_claims.source: memory (WPF Dispatcher priority and Win32 posted-message order)
outside_claims.if_wrong: A key pressed in the few-ms gap of a tick goes to the ListBox and does nothing (SC-254). That is filed for a person; it is not measurable here.

outside_claims.claim: On a recycling VirtualizingStackPanel, ObservableCollection.Move of the item whose container has keyboard focus unlinks that container and drops focus to the ListBox.
outside_claims.source: Spike 1: S3 0/10 and S4 3/10, with the mechanism shown by the refocus run. Spike 2: real MainWindow, r3.
outside_claims.if_wrong: An in-place diff would have been viable. Q-078 would still govern this slice, so only the filed keep-alive follow-up changes.

outside_claims.claim: After the scroll offset is restored, one TopLevelList.UpdateLayout() realises the containers at the restored offset. ItemContainerGenerator.ContainerFromItem then returns null only for rows outside it.
outside_claims.source: memory. Partly supported by spike 2's Loaded fallback, which focused a new container after UpdateLayout.
outside_claims.if_wrong: A scrolled focused row (AScrolledFocusedRowKeepsFocusAndOffset) is not refocused until a later tick. A second layout pass or a different realisation step would be needed.

outside_claims.claim: VirtualizingStackPanel keeps a keyboard-focused container realised even when it is out of view. FrameworkElement brings a newly keyboard-focused element into view, and with CanContentScroll=True that can shift the offset by up to one item for a partially visible row.
outside_claims.source: memory (VirtualizingStackPanel container cleanup; FrameworkElement.OnGotFocus calling BringIntoView)
outside_claims.if_wrong: If the first half is wrong, the UpdateLayout-first ordering is merely cautious. If the second half is right, 'the refresh never moves the viewport' has a one-row exception when the focused row ends partially visible. The scrolled-row Fact must then use a fully visible row and say so.

outside_claims.claim: An open ContextMenu holds keyboard focus inside its popup, so Keyboard.FocusedElement is not a TopLevelList container while a row menu is open.
outside_claims.if_wrong: The refocus could pull focus out of an open menu and close it every 250 ms, breaking SL-047's live-scan menu. AnOpenRowMenuSurvivesARefresh settles it. The fix would be one more capture condition: an open ContextMenu on the container.

outside_claims.claim: While the window is inactive, Keyboard.FocusedElement is null. On reactivation, WPF restores keyboard focus from the window's logical focus (FocusManager), which may still point at a container that a refresh detached.
outside_claims.if_wrong: Either way, the first Ctrl+Enter after returning from Explorer may do nothing until the person clicks or arrows onto a row, or until focus lands on the list and the next tick refocuses. Filed for the person's by-hand check.

outside_claims.claim: Setting SelectedItem from code does not move keyboard focus to the item's container. Arrow keys then start from the list.
outside_claims.source: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/7363777/arrow-keys-dont-work-after-programmatically-setting-listview-selecteditem. Also the investigation probe A2 (new container IsSelected=true, not keyboard-focused).
outside_claims.if_wrong: Refocusing the container would be unnecessary but harmless.

cross_domain_transfer.pattern: The view is rebuilt and re-sorted wholesale on every tick. After each rebuild the cursor is re-derived from a stable key (the PID), not kept by preserving row objects or screen positions.
cross_domain_transfer.rationale: Like htop, this app redraws a re-sorted list every 250 ms from an immutable snapshot. The 'follow by key' half transfers. The 'keep the node alive' half (React-style keyed reconciliation) does not: on a recycling VirtualizingStackPanel, a Move of the focused item disconnects its container (spikes 1 and 2). htop scrolls to follow the process; this design deliberately does not move the viewport.

invariants.precondition: The key is unique within one snapshot.
invariants.evidence: Root children have distinct exact names, and Ordinal comparison keeps case siblings apart (lesson #327).

invariants.precondition: The key is stable across the snapshots of one scan.
invariants.evidence: TopLevelTracker keeps rows in listing order, with row i = root child _first+i, and rebuilds only dirty rows (TopLevelTracker.cs:166-202). Path comes from the listing and does not change mid-scan.

invariants.precondition: The cursor is re-derived before the next input is acted on.
invariants.evidence: Spike 3: an Input-priority press queued straight after the swap ran after the Loaded restore, 30/30 per process. Spike 2 r3: the repro's press ran after a Loaded-priority refocus. The AKeyQueuedRightAfterTheSwapReachesTheRow Fact settles it on the real MainWindow. A real hardware keystroke in the gap (SC-254) is not measurable here.

invariants.precondition: The re-derived cursor's row has a realised container.
invariants.evidence: Spike 3's 20-row probe always kept r05 in view. This design lays out the restored offset before looking up the container. The scrolled-row Fact and the out-of-view Fact cover the in-view and out-of-view outcomes. A row out of view is accepted as selected but unfocused.

prior_art.pattern: After re-populating a list with new instances, re-select the item by its key string. Setting SelectedItem alone leaves keyboard focus off the item, so arrow keys and gestures start from the list; the item's container has to be focused.
Focus does not hold on a row when a ListView refreshes, and remembering it by index fails once rows move. That is why the design keys by Path, not by index.
After a list refresh the ListView itself takes keyboard focus: the same nearest-focusable-ancestor fallback measured on TopLevelList.

WinUI's ItemsRepeater had to fix focused elements not being recycled correctly on ItemsSource reassignment. Keeping focus across a source swap needs framework support that WPF's ListBox does not provide, so the app restores focus itself.
Accepted workaround: remember the selected or focused row by key, then after layout set SelectedItem, call UpdateLayout and focus the new container. Spike 3 measured this shape as go.

whats_new: ShowTopLevel captures, into closure locals before the ItemsSource swap, the selected row's Path, and the focused row's Path or whether the list itself had focus.

ShowTopLevel's existing Loaded callback gains a stale-array guard and an Ordinal reselect by Path. Only when focus was on the list or a row and WPF has dropped it onto TopLevelList, it then lays out the restored offset once and focuses the row's new ListBoxItem. A row not realised at that offset stays selected and unfocused, and the refresh never scrolls.
